opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I'd say they're still quite immature, and I think it's important to be upfront about that. If you compare alignment to a field like cryptography or even mainstream machine learning, we don't yet have a settled set of definitions that everyone agrees on and builds from. Words like "alignment," "honesty," "deception," or "corrigibility" get used constantly, but if you push on any one of them, people often mean somewhat different things, and the formal versions we do have tend to capture only a slice of what we actually care about.

That said, I don't think it's hopeless, and I'd distinguish between a few layers. There's the high-level problem statement: we want systems that do what we'd want them to do, even when we can't directly check their work. I think that framing is reasonably mature now. People broadly understand the issue of scalable oversight: as models get more capable, human evaluation becomes the bottleneck, and naive training on human feedback can reward things that look good rather than things that are good.

Then there's the layer of proposed approaches: debate, amplification, recursive reward modeling, interpretability, various forms of process supervision. Those are at a sort of adolescent stage. We have some theory, some toy results, and some empirical work with real language models, but we often can't yet say with confidence when a given method works and when it fails. With debate, for instance, there's a nice complexity-theoretic story about why it could, in principle, let a weak judge supervise a strong system. But the gap between that idealized story and what happens with actual humans and actual models is large. Humans have systematic biases, debaters can exploit obfuscation, and there are open questions about whether honest strategies actually win in practice.

The least mature layer, I'd say, is the connection between these methods and the safety guarantees we'd really want. We don't have a good way of saying "this system is safe enough to deploy at this capability level" with anything like the rigor you'd want for something this consequential. A lot of current practice rests on evaluations and red-teaming, which are valuable but are fundamentally about finding problems rather than establishing their absence.

So my overall assessment is that the concepts are maturing, and faster than they were five or ten years ago, partly because we now have capable models to experiment on. But we're still at the point where a careful theoretical argument can change people's minds about what the core problems even are. That's a sign of a young field. And it's one reason I think it's worth having more people with strong backgrounds in theory, whether complexity theory, game theory, or statistics, working alongside the empirical folks, because a lot of the remaining work is getting the concepts sharp enough that we know what we're actually trying to achieve.

r001.rationale: The response says alignment lacks settled, shared definitions and contrasts this with established fields such as cryptography and mainstream machine learning.

r002.rationale: It describes several proposed approaches and their limitations, but does not say that historical research has explored only a narrow portion of the available theoretical approaches.

r003.rationale: It calls sharpening concepts part of the remaining work, but does not identify defining them as low-hanging fruit.

r004.rationale: It advocates sharper concepts and theory alongside empirical work, but does not connect theoretically robust definitions to better predictions of empirical behavior.

fable-5.1.text:
I'd say they're immature, honestly, and I think it's worth being clear-eyed about that. A lot of the field's core concepts are still at the stage where we have a word for something and a rough intuition about what it means, but not a definition that would survive contact with a serious attempt to formalize it.

Take "alignment" itself. We use the word constantly, but if you push on it, you get several different things: the model doing what the user asks, the model doing what the user would want on reflection, the model behaving in ways that are good for the world, the model having some internal goal structure that's safe. Those come apart in practice, and the field hasn't really settled which one it's talking about, or how to trade them off when they conflict. The same is true of "deception," "corrigibility," "honesty." We have examples and counterexamples, but we don't have crisp criteria.

Compare that to a field like cryptography, which I think is a useful reference point. Cryptography has precise definitions, it has threat models, it has proofs that say "if this assumption holds, this adversary can't do that." Alignment is nowhere near that. We mostly have empirical observations about particular models, and a set of informal arguments about why things might go wrong at larger scale.

Now, I don't think that's a reason for despair. Most fields look like this early on. Physics was a mess before people figured out the right abstractions, and the right abstractions often come after a lot of empirical fumbling, not before. So I'd characterize where we are as: we're doing the empirical fumbling, we're collecting a lot of data about how models actually behave, and some of the conceptual work is starting to catch up. Things like scalable oversight, debate, interpretability have at least a sketch of a theoretical story behind them, even if the details are unsettled.

What worries me is less the immaturity per se and more the timeline. If we had fifty years, I'd be pretty relaxed. The question is whether we can get the concepts to a usable level of precision before the systems become capable enough that mistakes are very costly. And I think that means being somewhat opportunistic: taking the concepts that are closest to being formalizable, pushing on those, and being honest about where we're still just gesturing.

astra-6.text:
I think they’re still quite immature. We have words like “alignment” and “intent” and “oversight,” but those words can hide a lot of disagreement about what problem we’re actually trying to solve. You can agree that you want an AI to do what people want, and then immediately run into questions about which people, what counts as wanting something, and what happens when people don’t understand the consequences.

That doesn’t mean we can’t make progress. It means we should try to turn those broad ideas into precise questions: what information does the human have, what can the model do, and under what conditions does the proposed method fail? Then we can test pieces of the problem and improve our understanding.

I’d distinguish having a useful research direction from having a settled conceptual foundation. I think we have the former. I’m much less confident we have the latter.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a lot of the core concepts are still quite immature. We have words like “alignment” and “intent” and “values,” but we don’t yet know exactly how to turn those into precise questions that we can reliably answer. And sometimes using the same word makes it sound as though we agree more than we actually do.

That doesn’t mean we can’t make progress. You can take a particular failure mode, build a setup where you can study it, and test whether an approach helps. But I’d distinguish that kind of concrete progress from having a mature conceptual framework for the whole problem. I don’t think we have that yet.
